stories.title: Tim Walz Warns That Democrats Can Win And Still Lose
stories.text: LISTEN NOW: With the midterms less than a month away, some pundits and polls suggest Democrats have the election in the bag. But is that really true? David Sirota travels to Minnesota to speak with someone who knows the danger of election complacency and overconfidence: Democratic Gov. Tim Walz. Today on Lever Time , we’re airing David Sirota’s full conversation with Walz. They reflect on the choices that led to a 2024 presidential defeat for the Democrats, from the party’s stance on the genocide in Gaza to Kamala Harris’s decision to campaign with Republican Liz Cheney. Ahead of the 2026 midterms, what can we learn from Walz's experience? Does he believe the Democrats stand a chance? And what happens if the Democrats win and fail to deliver on their promises? stories.author: Matt Taibbi
stories.title: Note on Roger Waters and Other Superior Moral Beings
stories.text: Yesterday I wrote an article in defense of what the Soviets called “art for art’s sake” after Metallica frontman James Hetfield controversially declared his band’s agenda to be “love, energy, and heavy music, baby!” Former Pink Floyd lead singer Roger Waters, who declared Hetfield a “prick” who “can’t play a note,” was mentioned mainly for saying “‘I’m apolitical’ is not an option,” a stance with which I disagree. Waters responded: I’ve defended Roger Waters on speech issues multiple times in this space, and when he gets in trouble again, as he inevitably will, I’ll do so again. I bring it up only to note that his “useless idiot” salvo marks roughly the 958th time a left-leaning figure whom I’d publicly defended has denounced me as cowardly, compromised, immoral scum for failing to endorse their political opinions. But who cares about behaving with class when people are dying? The problem is the separation of artists into “political” and “apolitical” categories. stories.author: Drop Site team
stories.title: Encircled by War, Yemen's Taiz Residents Brace for Fighting and a Renewed Siege
stories.text: Ahmed Al-Issai, in his 60s, has resorted to living in the courtyard of Al-Thawrah Hospital in Taiz city, Yemen. TAIZ, Yemen—Like other residents of Taiz, Hael Mohammed is struggling to find food and other life essentials for his family as an escalating war between Ansarallah and a Saudi-led coalition draws in on the city. “No one can imagine how difficult the journey is just to find a propane cylinder or a bag of wheat in this city,” the 41-year-old pharmacist and father of three told Drop Site News. “Many food traders told me their stores have run out of wheat, rice, and other essentials. When I finally found wheat, it was nearly double its normal price.” Mohammed said that residents across Taiz are stockpiling food, fearing they could be trapped in their homes as the ground battles close in. The third largest city in Yemen, located in the southwestern highlands, Taiz has long been on the front line of Yemen’s civil war—and is now encircled by fighting. Taiz governorate consists of 23 districts, 20 of which are now under Ansarallah control. stories.author: Drop Site team
stories.title: Displaced Civilians Sifting for Gold in Sudan Killed in Bloody Drone Strike
stories.text: AD-DAMAZIN, Sudan—On the morning of October 9, Ahmed Ragab Abu Shina, 39, joined dozens of other displaced people digging for gold in a seasonal riverbed, known locally as a khor , near the Abu Shandi shelter in Sudan’s Blue Nile State. At around 9 a.m., a drone flew overhead from the south. No one knew whose it was, and no one thought it had come for them. Suddenly, an explosive shell landed in the middle of the khor , where men, women and children were working side by side. “After the shell fell, dozens went down, and whoever could flee fled,” Ragab told Drop Site News. “In those moments, no one knew where their family members or relatives were.” The strike killed 32 displaced people—26 women, four children and two elderly people—and wounded 43 others, according to Dr. Mustafa Jabrallah, Blue Nile State’s acting health minister. stories.author: The Lever team
stories.title: The $430 Million War Against Taxing The Rich
stories.text: This is a web version of The Lever ’s daily email newsletter. Income inequality is on the ballot this November, and in states across the country, citizens will vote directly on measures related to taxing the rich. Wealthy donors have emptied their pockets to try and sway voters in their direction, spending at least $430 million this election cycle either fighting ballot measures that would raise taxes on the richest Americans or supporting ones that keep taxes on the ultrawealthy low. Much of the attention has gone to California, where a first-of-its-kind billionaire tax has drawn the ire of Silicon Valley oligarchs and Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom — but voters in Colorado, Washington, and North Carolina will also have their say on a wealth tax this Election Day. In today’s Lever Daily , we’re tracking who’s dropping cash to block taxes on the rich, how much they’re spending, and which politicians are helping them. 🌴 California. In the Golden State alone, opponents have unloaded a “ carpet bomb ” of cash — more than $255 million — trying to defeat a ballot measure that would levy a one-time, 5 percent tax on residents with a net worth exceeding $1 billion.
